sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

# Surfing Pelican 🏄‍♂️🌊

An animated, **non-interactive** scene: a pelican in full surfing stance carving a
golden-hour swell, built with [three.js](https://threejs.org) and ES modules.

Just open `index.html` (or serve the folder) — there is nothing to click, the
pelican rides the whole loop by itself.

## Run it

```bash
npm install        # installs three
npm start          # vite-free dev server (see below) OR just serve the folder
```

Any static file server works:

```bash
npx serve .        # or: python3 -m http.server 8000
```

## How it is put together

| file        | what lives there                                                     |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `index.html`| markup, the vignette/caption styling, and the module entry           |
| `main.js`   | the whole scene (see below)                                          |
| `README.md` | this file                                                            |

No import maps, no CDN, no external assets — every texture is drawn on a
`<canvas>` in code.

### The wave field

`main.js` defines one wave field (a sum of three directional sine waves) and
reuses it in two places:

* **JavaScript** — `waveHeight()` / `waveNormal()` place the pelican, its board,
  the spray emitters and the sailboat exactly on the moving surface.
* **GLSL** — `waveGLSL()` emits the very same constants as shader code, so the
  ocean mesh and the physics agree to the millimetre.

The ocean is a 760 × 760 grid whose vertices are displaced in the vertex shader
(normals come from central differences of the same field). It stays centred on
the camera and slides in grid-sized steps, which keeps the surface continuous
while the geometry never has to be rebuilt.

The water shader mixes a depth gradient, a fresnel sky reflection (the shared
`skyColor()` function is also used by the sky dome), sun glitter, animated foam
on the crests and whitecaps on steep faces, then fades into exponential-squared
fog that matches the horizon haze.

### The pelican

Assembled from primitives (spheres, tubes, cones and two extruded plan-forms —
one for the surfboard outline, one for the wings) into a small hierarchy:

```
ride        — world placement: wave height, board orientation, bank into turns
 └ body     — surf stance, bob, crouch, lean
    ├ torso / belly / tail
    ├ neck (S-curve) → head → beak, pouch, eyes
    ├ wingL / wingR — pivots that flap and adjust while carving
    └ legs + webbed feet on the deck
```

The board orientation is built from an orthonormal frame (forward, wave normal,
side) each frame, tilted toward the inside of the turn by a bank angle derived
from the closed-form curvature of the oval circuit — so it leans into the corners
instead of sliding around them.

Around it: a camera that swings in from a wide establishing shot and then
follows with damping and a gentle handheld float, a point-sprite spray system
(rooster tail off the tail, rail spray while carving), seagulls orbiting on
their own schedules and a small sailboat bobbing far out on the swell.

## Packaging

The page is bundled into a single self-contained `index.html` with esbuild:

```bash
esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=... 
```

Everything is either bundled or generated in code, so the result runs offline in
a sandboxed iframe with no network, storage or cookies.

## Surfing Pelican — animated, non-interactive three.js scene

**Files** (all inside the current directory):
- **`index.html`** — entry point: canvas container, vignette + title caption (CSS only), and `<script type="module" src="./main.js">`
- **`main.js`** — the whole scene as ES modules (`import * as THREE from "three"`, no CDN, no import maps)
- **`README.md`** — how to run it and how the pieces fit together
- `package.json` / `package-lock.json` / `node_modules` — `three@0.186.1` installed via npm

**What's in the scene**
- **Ocean**: a 760 × 760, 300-segment grid whose vertices are displaced in GLSL by a sum of three directional waves; normals come from central differences of the same field. The shader mixes a depth gradient, fresnel sky reflection, sun glitter, animated foam on crests/whitecaps, and distance fog that fades into the *actual* sky colour so the horizon never shows a seam. The mesh slides with the camera in grid-sized steps while waves stay sampled in world space, so it's continuous and never rebuilt.
- **Pelican**: primitives assembled into a hierarchy — surfboard (extruded outline with rounded rails + canvas-generated candy-stripe deck), tapered pear-shaped body, S-curve neck, head with beak/pouch/eyes, spread wings with dark tips that flap in bursts, legs and webbed feet. It rides an oval circuit, its board frame built each frame from the wave normal and a bank angle derived from the ellipse's curvature (it leans *into* the turns), plus bob, crouch, head scanning.
- **Around it**: a camera that swings in from a wide establishing shot then follows with damping and handheld float; a point-sprite spray system (rooster tail + rail spray, custom shader with per-particle alpha/size); six seagulls on independent orbits; a small distant sailboat bobbing on the same wave field.

**Key trick**: the wave field is defined once in JS and emitted as GLSL from the same constants (`waveGLSL()`), so the physics placement and the rendered surface agree exactly.

**Verified**: `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` succeeds, and I smoke-tested the bundled page in headless Chrome (SwiftShader) — no page errors, no shader warnings, no failed requests, and correct golden-hour renders checked over a full lap (sun glitter path, spray trail, seagulls, sailboat). All test artifacts were removed; no network, storage or cookies are used, so it will run offline in a sandboxed iframe.
